from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Points in space are absolute.",
            "A coordinate system provides their numerical address.",
            "Changing the grid changes the coordinates.",
            "The point remains fixed in space.",
            "Perspective defines our numerical description."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Intuition: Points vs. Perspectives", lecture_lines)
        
        origin = Dot(self.grid["F1"], color=WHITE)
        point_A = Dot(self.grid["B3"], color=WHITE)
        point_B = Dot(self.grid["D5"], color=WHITE)
        
        line_OA = Line(origin.get_center(), point_A.get_center(), color=WHITE)
        line_OB = Line(origin.get_center(), point_B.get_center(), color=WHITE)
        
        label_A = Text("A", font_size=20, color=WHITE).next_to(point_A, UP, buff=0.1)
        label_B = Text("B", font_size=20, color=WHITE).next_to(point_B, UP, buff=0.1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Points in space are absolute.
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        self.play(FadeIn(point_A), FadeIn(point_B), Write(label_A), Write(label_B))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # A coordinate system provides their numerical address.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FF00FF")
        self.play(FadeIn(line_OA), FadeIn(line_OB), FadeIn(origin))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Changing the grid changes the coordinates.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FFFF")
        self.play(point_A.animate.set_color("#00FFFF"), point_B.animate.set_color("#00FFFF"))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # The point remains fixed in space.
        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.play(Flash(point_A), Flash(point_B))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # Perspective defines our numerical description.
        self.lecture[3].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#00FF00")
        self.wait(1)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "A basis B defines our coordinate system.",
            "Any vector is a linear combination of B.",
            "The Change of Basis matrix P is a dictionary.",
            "P maps B-basis coordinates to standard ones.",
            "P uses basis vectors as columns."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Defining the Basis Matrix", lecture_lines)
        
        # Define objects
        vec_i = Vector([1, 0.5], color=YELLOW)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===

        self.place_at_grid(vec_i, 'B2', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.place_at_grid(vec_j, 'B4', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(Create(vec_i), Create(vec_j))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.place_at_grid(matrix_m, 'D3', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(FadeIn(matrix_m))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(GREEN))
        new_vec_i = Vector([0.8, 0.8], color=GREEN)
        new_vec_j = Vector([-0.8, 0.8], color=GREEN)
        self.play(
            ReplacementTransform(vec_i, new_vec_i),
            ReplacementTransform(vec_j, new_vec_j)
        )
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Coordinates in basis B are [v]B.",
            "The formula [v]std = P[v]B is the bridge.",
            "Matrix P represents the transformation mechanism.",
            "Numerical representations change as the grid shifts.",
            "The underlying vector remains invariant."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Transformation Mechanics", lecture_lines)
        
        # Elements
        vec_p = Vector([1, 2], color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(vec_p, 'C3')
        label_p = MathTex(r"v", color=WHITE).next_to(vec_p.get_end(), UP)
        
        formula = MathTex(r"[v]_{std} = P[v]_B", color=YELLOW)
        self.place_at_grid(formula, 'B5')

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(vec_p), Write(label_p))
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(YELLOW))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        vec_transformed = Vector([2, 1], color=PURPLE)
        self.place_at_grid(vec_transformed, 'D3')
        label_transformed = MathTex(r"v_B", color=PURPLE).next_to(vec_transformed.get_end(), DOWN)
        self.play(Create(vec_transformed), Write(label_transformed))
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(PURPLE))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        rect = SurroundingRectangle(formula, color="#00FFFF", buff=0.1)
        self.play(Create(rect))
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color("#00FFFF"))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(FadeOut(vec_p), FadeOut(label_p))
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["What if we have standard coordinates?", "We use the inverse matrix, P inverse.", "Basis vectors must be linearly independent."]
        self.setup_layout("Inverting the Perspective", lecture_lines)
        
        # Elements
        matrix_m = MathTex(r"M = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}", color=WHITE)
        matrix_inv = MathTex(r"M^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad-bc} \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}", color=RED)
        independent_text = Text("Linearly Independent", color=YELLOW)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(self.place_at_grid(matrix_m, 'B2', scale_factor=1.2)))
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(self.place_at_grid(matrix_inv, 'D2', scale_factor=1.0)))
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(RED))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(self.place_at_grid(independent_text, 'F3', scale_factor=0.8)))
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.wait(2)

sections.title: The Intuition: Points vs. Perspectives
sections.content: Establish prerequisite: A coordinate system is just a grid. Explain that a point in space is absolute, but its numerical 'address' depends on the axes (basis) we choose. Use an animation of a character (a robot) moving across a grid.
sections.example: Imagine a robot standing on a square grid. If we rotate the floor, the robot hasn't moved, but its 'x' and 'y' coordinates relative to the new walls have changed.

sections.title: Defining the Basis Matrix
sections.content: Introduce the Change of Basis Matrix (P). Explain that if basis B = {v1, v2}, any vector can be written as a linear combination: v = c1v1 + c2v2. Visually represent this as a 'Translation Dictionary' that maps coordinates from the B-basis to the Standard basis.
sections.example: If Basis B is made of two vectors at 45 degrees, the matrix P uses those vectors as columns. P converts 'coordinates in B' into 'standard coordinates'.

sections.title: The Transformation Mechanics
sections.content: Focus on the formula [v]_std = P[v]_B. Use a flow animation: a vector in space, a coordinate system grid shifting, and the matrix multiplication acting as the bridge between the two numerical representations.
sections.example: A GPS coordinate system vs. a local park coordinate system. The same landmark (the vector) has different numbers, linked by the matrix P.

sections.title: Inverting the Perspective
sections.content: Address the inverse process: How to find coordinates in basis B if we have the standard ones. Introduce P^-1. Emphasize that switching basis is reversible as long as the basis vectors are linearly independent.
sections.example: A camera zooming out: If you know how the world looks from the camera's tilted angle (B), you can use P^-1 to calculate how the world looks from the 'upright' standard view.

sections.title: Conclusion and Summary
sections.content: Summarize the 'Change of Basis' as a simple change in perspective. Reinforce that the vector remains invariant (it doesn't change length or direction), only our description of it changes.
sections.example: Final visual: A cat sitting in the center of the room. Two observers stand at different corners, recording the cat's position using different rulers. The cat is the 'vector', the observers' setups are the 'bases'.
